fields.title: The Retry That Cures and the Retry That Kills
fields.keyTakeaway: Retries without exponential backoff and jitter destroy an overloaded service, while a circuit breaker turns a timeout wait into an instant fallback.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A request fails — should you retry immediately? And what if it fails for a thousand clients at once?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Naive retries are a classic reason why a short-term slowdown turns into a half-hour outage. The mechanism is non-obvious: every participant behaves rationally, yet the system collapses.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The service slows down. A thousand clients don't wait and retry. Load doubles. Slowdown worsens. They retry again. This is a [[retry-storm|retry storm]], and it can finish off a service that would have recovered on its own.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[exponential-backoff|Exponential backoff]].** The pause grows: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds. Gives time to recover.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[jitter|Jitter]].** Random addition. Without it, all clients dropping off at once will retry simultaneously — the same [[thundering-herd|thundering herd effect]] from `SC1-N1-L2`. With jitter, retries are smeared out.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Attempt limit.** Usually three. Beyond that — failure with a clear message.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The fourth tool works at a different level — **[[circuit-breaker|circuit breaker]]**. If the failure rate exceeds a threshold, we stop calling altogether and immediately return a fallback. After a while, we try one request ([[half-open|half-open state]]); if it succeeds, we return to normal.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The circuit breaker provides two things: the failed service gets breathing room, and our product responds instantly instead of waiting for a timeout. It is what prevents the cascade from `SC1-N3-L2`.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: The product part is **what to return while tripped.** This is a fallback from the degradation matrix, and it must exist in advance.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: A separate rule: **only idempotent operations can be retried.** Direct connection to `IN2-N3`: without an idempotency key, retries create duplicates.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Retry policy introduced after the third cascade:
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/0/3: No — critical, wait until the end
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Threshold logic: the less important the service, the faster we trip. Recommendations turn off at 20% failures because it is cheaper to show popular items than to wait.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: An incident that showed the cost of jitter: during a brief network glitch, all application instances retried at exactly 2 seconds simultaneously. A spike 8 times above normal crashed a service that had already recovered by then. ±30% jitter removed the effect completely.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: A circuit breaker can trip due to an error in defining failure and disable a working service. Threshold and window require tuning, and the circuit breaker state is a separate metric on monitoring.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Retries without exponential backoff and jitter destroy an overloaded service, while a circuit breaker turns a timeout wait into an instant fallback.
